897.title: Work with excellence
897.hook: a hadith: God loves that when you do a work, you do it with excellence (al-Bayhaqi)
897.howItsDone: Muslims speak of ihsan both in worship, praying as though seeing God, and in daily work, and teachers often cite the hadith that God loves work done with excellence when talking about jobs, crafts and study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hadith about bread you earn yourself. Your line was by my own hands. What did you eat that came from your own work? Today, the same tradition asks how the work is done. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

The underside of a drawer. Nobody will ever see it. The customer opens the drawer, takes out a spoon, and never once turns it over. And still some carpenters sand that hidden side smooth, the same as the front. Ask why, and the answer may have nothing to do with money. Muslims have a narration that speaks to exactly this. It's recorded in the hadith collection of al-Bayhaqi, and it says, in paraphrase, that when one of you does a piece of work, God loves that it be done with excellence. Not the work people watch. Any work. Today's word is the name for that kind of care.
screen: `THE UNDERSIDE OF A DRAWER.` → `NOBODY SEES IT.` → `GOD LOVES WORK DONE WELL.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Ihsan is an Arabic word put into English as excellence, or doing what is beautiful. It comes up in a scene recorded in Sahih Muslim. A stranger in very white clothes sits down knee to knee with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and asks him questions. What is islam? What is iman, faith? And then, what is ihsan? The answer, in paraphrase: to worship God as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, to know that He sees you. After the stranger leaves, the Prophet tells his companions that it was the angel Gabriel, come to teach them their religion. So in this teaching, ihsan begins as a way of standing before God. Second, it doesn't stay in the prayer hall. Another hadith in Sahih Muslim says God has prescribed ihsan in all things. And the example it gives is not a mosque or a sermon. It's a knife. When you slaughter an animal, sharpen your blade and spare the animal. Excellence reaches all the way down to the edge of a butcher's knife. Third, the narration from al-Bayhaqi takes it into the workshop: God loves that when you do a work, you do it well. Put the three side by side and a picture forms. Muslim teachers describe ihsan as doing a thing as though it's seen, because, in their faith, it is. In that telling, the underside of the drawer is not hidden from God. Fourth, what this asks of an ordinary afternoon. It isn't perfectionism, the anxious kind that never finishes. It's attention. The email read once more before sending. The bandage put on gently. The rice washed properly. Excellence, in this telling, is less about being the best and more about not cutting the corner nobody would notice.
screen: `AS THOUGH YOU SEE HIM.` · `IHSAN IN ALL THINGS.` · `GOD LOVES WORK DONE WELL.` · `ATTENTION, NOT PERFECTIONISM.` · then, large: `IHSAN.`

segments.voice: Make the sitting itself the piece of work. Set your feet with care. Let the back lengthen, not stiff, just upright. Place your hands where they can rest, the way a carpenter sets down a finished drawer. Now give the next breath your full attention: the start of it, the turn at the top, the long way out. Then the next one. When the mind wanders off, come back without fuss, the way you would sand one more stroke on a side nobody sees. If you pray, you can sit as though seen, in your own tradition's way. If you don't, simply let the breath have your care. The bell holds the time.
Ihsan. An Arabic word for excellence, doing what is beautiful, as though seen by God. Today's word.
Your line: excellence. Today, do one task excellently, including the part nobody will check. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

898.title: Right livelihood
898.hook: the Buddha names trades to avoid, such as dealing in weapons and poisons (Anguttara Nikaya 5.177)
898.carry: harm into the hands of someone else
898.howItsDone: Buddhists list right livelihood as one step of the noble eightfold path, and Buddhist teachers often raise it when lay followers ask how to choose or carry out their work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ihsan: work done with excellence, as though seen. Your line was excellence. Which task got your full care? Yesterday asked how the work is done. Today asks what the work does. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

Weapons. Living beings. Meat. Intoxicants. Poison. That's the whole list, and it's short. In a discourse kept in the Anguttara Nikaya, one of the collections of the Buddha's teachings, he names five kinds of trade that a lay follower should not take up. He doesn't name priests or kings or bankers. He names what changes hands. A sword. A living being sold. A jar of something that clouds the mind. A vial of something that kills. It's a list about what your work puts into the world. Today's word is the step of the Buddhist path it belongs to.
screen: `FIVE TRADES, ONE SHORT LIST.` → `WHAT CHANGES HANDS.` → `WHAT YOUR WORK PUTS OUT.`

segments.voice: First, where it sits. In the teaching Buddhists call the turning of the wheel of the Dhamma, the Buddha lays out the noble eightfold path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Right livelihood comes just after speech and action. So a job is not set apart from the spiritual life. How you earn is part of the path, the same as how you speak. Second, the list itself. In the Anguttara, the five trades are dealing in weapons, in living beings, in meat, in intoxicants, and in poison. Notice the thread running through them. Each one, in its own way, puts harm into the hands of someone else. Third, who it's for. The Buddha speaks these words to his monks, but the rule isn't about monks. It's about lay followers, people with households and bills. It doesn't tell them to stop working. It tells them which work to leave alone. Buddhist teachers differ on how far to take it today. Some read the list closely and keep to it. Others treat it as a direction more than a fence, and ask a wider question of any job: who does this hurt, and could it hurt less? Fourth, why this is harder than it sounds. A list like this can seem far from an office or a kitchen. But the question underneath the list goes everywhere. A sales target that pushes someone into a loan they can't carry. Food that's cheap because someone, somewhere, is paid too little. The list is short. The question it leaves behind is not.
screen: `A STEP ON THE EIGHTFOLD PATH.` · `WEAPONS, BEINGS, MEAT, DRINK, POISON.` · `A RULE FOR PEOPLE WITH JOBS.` · `WHO DOES THIS HURT?` · then, large: `RIGHT LIVELIHOOD.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath slow. Let one piece of your work come to mind, just one. A product you sell, a message you send, a meal you cook, a decision you sign off on. Hold it the way you'd hold a cup, turning it slowly in your hands. Ask the discourse's question of it: does anything harmful change hands here? Often the answer may be no. If something does come up, don't argue with it. Let it sit beside the breath. Then ask a smaller question: what one change would make it a little less harmful? If you pray, you can bring this question in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Right livelihood. A step on the Buddha's eightfold path: earning a living in a way that does not deal in harm. Today's word.
Your line: harm into the hands of someone else. Today, ask once of your work: does this harm anyone, and could it harm less? Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

899.title: No work, no food
899.hook: the Chan master Baizhang: a day without work is a day without food (Chan tradition)
899.howItsDone: In Chan and Zen monasteries, monks and teachers share manual work such as cooking, cleaning and gardening as part of daily practice, and Baizhang's saying is often quoted about it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha's short list of trades to leave alone. Your line was harm into the hands of someone else. When you asked whether your work harms, what did you find? Today, a teacher who wouldn't stop working. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.
screen: `HARM INTO THE HANDS OF SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: The tools are gone. The hoe, the rake, whatever he used in the fields, hidden somewhere by his own students. They meant well. Their teacher was old, the Chan tradition says, and still went out every day to work the land beside the monks, and they wanted him to rest. So they hid his tools. He didn't argue. He didn't search. He just didn't eat that day. When they asked him why, the answer has been passed down in Chan and Zen communities: a day without work is a day without food. The teacher was Baizhang. Today's word is the first half of his saying.
screen: `THE TOOLS ARE HIDDEN.` → `HE DOESN'T EAT.` → `A DAY WITHOUT WORK.`

segments.voice: First, who Baizhang is in the story. Chan is the Chinese school of Buddhism known in Japan as Zen. Tradition remembers Baizhang as a Chan master who shaped how a Chan monastery ran day to day: when to sit, when to eat, and when to work. In this telling, the monks didn't only meditate. They farmed, cooked, swept and hauled, and the teacher worked with them. Second, what the saying is not. It's easy to hear no work, no food as a threat, the kind a boss might shout. But in the story, Baizhang says it of himself. Nobody punishes him. He simply keeps his own rule. The sharpness is aimed inward. Third, a difference worth saying plainly. In other Buddhist communities, monks live on alms, food given by lay people, and that giving is itself a practice for the givers. The Chan way of working the land grew up alongside that, as a different arrangement, not a correction of it. Both are ways of keeping a community fed and a mind awake. Fourth, what it might mean at a kitchen table. In a monastery, work is shared. Nobody's job is beneath anyone. Somebody washes the pots, and the teacher might be the one with his sleeves rolled up. At home, the same question waits by the sink. Who does the dishes? Who takes out the trash? Baizhang's saying doesn't ask you to earn your dinner in money. It asks whether you've done your share of what keeps the place running.
screen: `A CHAN MASTER IN THE FIELDS.` · `A RULE HE KEPT FOR HIMSELF.` · `ALMS, OR THE HOE: BOTH FEED.` · `YOUR SHARE AT HOME.` · then, large: `NO WORK, NO FOOD.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle and the breath slow down. Baizhang's rule pointed at himself, not at the monks. Try that turn. Think of one thing you wish other people at home would do. Rinse the cup. Close the cupboard. Put the shoes away. Notice the small heat of that wish, without scolding it. Now turn it around, the way he did. Make it a rule for you alone, just for today, and tell nobody. Hold the rule quietly while the breath comes and goes. If you pray, you can bring your household into it, in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
No work. The first half of Baizhang's saying, a day without work is a day without food: a rule he kept for himself. Today's word.
Your line: sleeves rolled up. Today, before dinner, do your share of the chores, and maybe one more. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

900.title: Chop wood, carry water
900.hook: Layman Pang's verse: the marvelous is in carrying water and chopping wood (Chan tradition)
900.carry: fully present to the weight of the bucket
900.howItsDone: In Chan and Zen practice, daily chores such as cooking, cleaning and carrying are treated as part of meditation, and Layman Pang's verse is often quoted to make the point.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baizhang and the hidden tools. Your line was sleeves rolled up. Which chore did you take on? Today, another voice from the same Chan world, and it isn't a monk's. Day nine hundred.

What would count as a miracle in your house? A bill that pays itself? A teenager who empties the dishwasher unasked? In the Chan tradition, a man known as Layman Pang was asked by his teacher what his days had been like, and his answer, as it's handed down, is a short verse. Its punch line, in paraphrase: my supernatural power, my marvelous activity, is carrying water and hauling firewood. That's it. No flying. No reading minds. A bucket and a bundle of sticks. Today's word comes from that verse, in the shape people now pass it around: chop wood.
screen: `A MIRACLE IN YOUR HOUSE?` → `NO FLYING, NO MIND-READING.` → `A BUCKET AND SOME STICKS.`

segments.voice: First, who's speaking. Layman means he wasn't a monk. Chan tradition remembers Pang as a householder, with a family, who studied with Chan teachers and is remembered for sharp, plain answers. So the verse comes from someone living an ordinary life, not from behind monastery walls. Second, the turn in the verse. It opens by saying his daily affairs are nothing special, then reaches for some very big words, supernatural powers, marvelous functioning, and attaches them to the dullest jobs in the house. The joke is serious. Whatever is wonderful about awakening, the verse says, it shows up in the bucket and the firewood, not somewhere else. Third, the saying it turned into. You may have heard a version that goes: before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water; after enlightenment, chop wood, carry water. That neat line gets passed around, and it shares Layman Pang's spirit, but the words aren't his. His verse, as it's handed down, speaks of hauling firewood, not chopping it. Fourth, what changes if nothing changes. The chores stay the same. The water still has to be carried. What the verse points to is the one carrying it. A person can haul water while thinking of a hundred other places. Or a person can haul water. In Chan, that second way of doing it, fully present to the weight of the bucket, is not a step toward the practice. It is the practice.
screen: `A LAYMAN, NOT A MONK.` · `GRAND WORDS FOR DULL JOBS.` · `A SAYING, NOT HIS WORDS.` · `JUST CARRY THE WATER.` · then, large: `CHOP WOOD.`

segments.voice: Sit easily, and let the breath come and go. Choose one chore you'll do after the bell. Washing a pan. Folding a towel. Watering a plant. Then leave it there, and come back to this. Sitting is a chore too. Feel the weight of the body in the seat, the way a bucket pulls on the arm. Feel the breath carried in and carried out. When the mind leaves for a hundred other places, notice where it went, and pick the bucket back up. Let it be nothing special, and see whether that's the same as dull. If you pray, you can offer the chore in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Chop wood. From Layman Pang's Chan verse: the marvelous is found in carrying water and firewood, in the plain work of a day. Today's word.
Your line: fully present to the weight of the bucket. Today, do one chore as if it were marvelous, and let it be only that chore while you do it. Day nine hundred.

901.title: The bell-stand maker
901.hook: Woodworker Qing fasts until he forgets praise and reward, then carves (Zhuangzi 19)
901.howItsDone: Readers of the Zhuangzi, including Daoist teachers and students of Chinese philosophy, often turn to Qing's story when talking about craft, focus and working without attachment to reward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Layman Pang and his bucket of water. Your line was fully present to the weight of the bucket. Did one chore become, even for a minute, only that chore? Today, a woodworker in the Chinese book called the Zhuangzi. Day nine hundred one.
screen: `FULLY PRESENT TO THE WEIGHT OF THE BUCKET.`

segments.voice: A wooden stand for hanging bells, finished and set out where people can see it. In the story, everyone who looks at it is startled. It seems too good for human hands, as if spirits made it. The ruler of Lu sees it too, and he questions the woodworker, a man named Qing. The ruler wants the secret. What technique? What training? What trick? Qing's answer, in the Chinese book called the Zhuangzi, isn't about chisels at all. It's about what he had to forget before he picked one up. Today's word is the craftsman himself: Qing.
screen: `TOO GOOD FOR HUMAN HANDS.` → `THE RULER WANTS THE SECRET.` → `IT ISN'T ABOUT CHISELS.`

segments.voice: First, the answer begins humbly. Qing says, in paraphrase, I'm only a workman, what art could I have? But there is one thing. Before he makes a bell-stand, he fasts, to make his mind still. Second, what the fast takes away. After three days, the text says, he no longer thinks of congratulations, reward, rank or pay. After five days, he no longer thinks of praise or blame, of being skillful or clumsy. After seven days, he forgets even his own limbs and body. And at that point, he says, even the ruler's court has dropped out of his mind. Notice the order. The first thing to go is the paycheck. The next is the audience. Then the self who wanted both. Third, what's left when they're gone. Only then does Qing walk into the forest. He looks at the trees, at their natural shape, until he finds one where he can already see the bell-stand inside it. Then he sets his hand to it. If he can't see it, he leaves the tree alone. The Zhuangzi calls this, in paraphrase, heaven meeting heaven: what's natural in the worker meeting what's natural in the wood. Fourth, why this still speaks to a modern desk. Work today can come with a prize always in view: the review, the likes, the raise, the boss walking past. Qing's story doesn't say rewards are evil. It says they get in the way of seeing. Work done while watching the audience is work done half-looking. The bell-stand that startled everyone came from someone who, for a while, had stopped caring whether it would.
screen: `I'M ONLY A WORKMAN.` · `PAY, THEN PRAISE, THEN SELF.` · `HE SEES IT IN THE TREE.` · `ONE EYE ON THE PRIZE.` · then, large: `THE BELL-STAND MAKER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath lengthen a little. Choose a piece of work ahead of you today. Now, like Qing, set things down one at a time. First, what you'll get for it. Let that go. Then, what people will say about it. Let that go too. Then even the worry about whether you're good enough. Let it go. What's left is the task itself, and the material in front of you. Rest there. If you pray, you can bring the work in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Qing. The woodworker in the Zhuangzi who fasted until he forgot reward and praise, then saw the bell-stand inside the tree. Today's word.
Your line: forget the prize. Today, do one piece of work once without thinking about who will praise it. Day nine hundred one.

902.title: Forgets to eat
902.hook: Confucius describes himself as someone so eager to learn he forgets his food (Analects 7.18)
902.howItsDone: Readers of the Analects, in Confucian schools and families and in classrooms, turn to this passage as Confucius's own picture of a life given to learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Qing the woodworker, who fasted until reward and praise fell away. Your line was forget the prize. Today, another kind of forgetting, from another Chinese teacher. Day nine hundred two.

Somebody asks your friend what you're really like, and your friend says nothing. Just stands there. Later, you hear about it. That's the scene in the Analects, the book of Confucius's sayings. A nobleman, the Duke of She, asks one of Confucius's students, Zilu, what kind of man his teacher is. Zilu doesn't answer. When Confucius finds out, he doesn't scold. He tells Zilu what he could have said. And the self-portrait he offers isn't of a sage or a statesman. It's a portrait Confucius offers of himself. Today's word is the student who stayed silent: Zilu.
screen: `WHAT'S HE REALLY LIKE?` → `ZILU SAYS NOTHING.` → `A MAN WHO FORGETS TO EAT.`

segments.voice: First, the description, in paraphrase. Why didn't you tell him, Confucius says, that I'm simply a man who, in his eagerness to learn, forgets his food; who, in the joy of it, forgets his worries; and who doesn't notice old age coming on? Three forgettings. Food. Sorrow. Age. Second, what's being chased. The line itself just says eagerness, but Legge and the commentators read it as eagerness to learn. Not power, not money. Learning, the steady work of study and practice that runs through the Analects. For Confucius, that work wasn't a chore to get through. In this passage, it's what he loses himself in. Third, notice the joy. He doesn't say he forgets food because he's grimly disciplined. He says the joy of it makes him forget his troubles. The eagerness comes first, and the forgetting follows. Nobody has to hide his tools or take away his plate. The hours just go. Fourth, how this sits next to yesterday. Qing the woodworker had to fast for days to forget reward and praise. Confucius describes something that arrives on its own when the work itself is loved. Two different roads to the same quiet place, where the clock and the stomach go silent for a while. And it's worth saying the honest part: the Analects doesn't recommend skipping meals. Elsewhere it records Confucius as careful about his food. This is a portrait of absorption, not a rule about lunch. A version of it can turn up anywhere. A puzzle, a garden, a song, a page of notes, and suddenly the window has gone dark.
screen: `FOOD, SORROW, AGE: FORGOTTEN.` · `WHAT HE CHASES IS LEARNING.` · `JOY COMES FIRST.` · `ABSORPTION, NOT A RULE.` · then, large: `FORGETS TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle into its own rhythm. Think back to a time you lost track of the hours doing something. Maybe recently, maybe long ago. What were you doing? Where were you sitting? What did your hands do? Let that memory fill in. Then ask: is there something like that within reach today, even for twenty minutes? Choose it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Zilu. The student who didn't answer when asked what kind of man Confucius was, and what Confucius told him he could have said. Today's word.
Your line: forget the hours. Today, lose yourself in one task, long enough that you look up surprised at the time. Day nine hundred two.

903.title: What it costs in life
903.hook: Thoreau: the cost of a thing is the amount of life exchanged for it (Walden 1)
903.howItsDone: Readers of Walden, including people interested in simple living, quote Thoreau's measure of cost in life when weighing purchases, jobs and the hours they ask for.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zilu's question, and Confucius, a man who forgets to eat. Your line was forget the hours. Did a task swallow the clock? Today, a writer who counted those hours very carefully. Day nine hundred three.

A new pair of shoes, and a price on the tag. Is that what they cost? Henry David Thoreau would ask a different question: how many hours of your life did those shoes take? At the start of Walden, his book about living by a pond in the Massachusetts woods, Thoreau sits down to do some accounts. Not just in money, though he lists that too, down to the nails. He's after a different ledger. He writes a sentence that turns every price tag around: "the cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it, immediately or in the long run." That's today's word.
screen: `A PRICE TAG.` → `HOW MANY HOURS?` → `A DIFFERENT LEDGER.`

segments.voice: First, the word he chooses. Not money, not effort. Life. Thoreau knows a dollar is really a stand-in for something else: the hours spent earning it, hours that don't come back. So the honest price of anything is paid in those hours. Second, the long run. Notice the last words: immediately or in the long run. Some things cost life up front. Others cost it slowly: the bigger house that needs the longer commute, the payments that keep you at a job you'd leave. Thoreau wants both counted. Third, a story he tells to make the point. Thoreau imagines racing a friend to a town some distance away. The friend will work for the train fare, then ride. Thoreau will set out on foot right now. He says, in paraphrase, that he'll get there first, because by the time the friend has earned the fare, the walker has already arrived. It's a joke, and it isn't. The train looks faster until you price it in life. Fourth, what he does not say. Thoreau isn't telling everyone to move to a cabin. He says plainly in Walden that he doesn't want anyone to adopt his way of living. His point is the arithmetic, done honestly, by each person, for their own life. And the sum can come out either way. Some things are worth every hour they cost: a tool that lasts, a trip to see someone you love, a gift. Thoreau's ledger doesn't forbid spending life. It asks that the spending be chosen, with the hours counted, rather than slipping away while nobody looks at the bill.
screen: `NOT MONEY: LIFE.` · `NOW, OR IN THE LONG RUN.` · `THE WALKER ARRIVES FIRST.` · `DO YOUR OWN ARITHMETIC.` · then, large: `WHAT IT COSTS IN LIFE.`

segments.voice: Sit easily, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing you bought recently, or one you're thinking of buying. See it clearly. Now, gently, do Thoreau's sum. Roughly how many hours of work did it take, or will it take? Hold that number in mind next to the thing itself. Don't judge it. Maybe it's worth every hour. Maybe not. Just let the two sit side by side. If you pray, you can bring the question into your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Walden. Thoreau's book about living by a pond, where he measures the cost of a thing in the life it takes to earn it. Today's word.
Your line: chosen, with the hours counted. Today, price one purchase in hours instead of dollars, and see if the number changes your mind. Day nine hundred three.

fork.setup: you and a friend both want to reach a town some distance away. your friend will work to earn the train fare, then ride. what does Thoreau choose?
options: work alongside the friend and ride too.
set out on foot right now.
stay home; it isn't worth the trip.
fork.reveal: Thoreau walks, and says he'll arrive first: by the time the fare is earned, the walker is already there.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quote about things being expensive.
what it means: the real price of a thing is the hours of life you trade to get it, now or later.
what a scholar hears: Walden's first chapter, Economy, where Thoreau keeps accounts and turns a cost into a measure of life.
